Cyberpunk 2077 is nothing short of a monumental achievement in modern gaming. Its meticulously crafted open world, breathtaking visual fidelity, and extraordinarily immersive atmosphere set a benchmark that few titles can even aspire to reach. Night City is not merely a backdrop for the narrative; it is a living, breathing metropolis, teeming with moral ambiguity, social stratification, technological obsession, and the haunting consequences of unchecked corporate power.

What truly distinguishes the game, however, is its narrative sophistication. Beneath its dazzling neon lights and futuristic spectacle lies a profoundly human story about identity, mortality, freedom, and the desperate pursuit of meaning in an increasingly dehumanised world. Its characters are remarkably nuanced, its dialogue often incisive, and its most emotionally resonant moments linger long after the credits roll.

Visually, Cyberpunk 2077 is nothing less than extraordinary. The interplay of neon illumination, atmospheric fog, intricate environmental detail, and sophisticated lighting techniques creates an aesthetic that is simultaneously mesmerising and unsettling. Night City feels as though it has been ripped from the darkest, most compelling visions of the future and brought to life with astonishing technical precision.

Ultimately, Cyberpunk 2077 transcends the boundaries of conventional entertainment. It is an ambitious, thought-provoking, and occasionally heartbreaking exploration of what it means to remain human in a world that increasingly treats humanity as a commodity. Few games manage to combine such artistic ambition, narrative depth, and technological brilliance so convincingly. Cyberpunk 2077 is not merely a game worth experiencing; it is an experience that exemplifies the extraordinary artistic potential of the medium itself.

After over 600 hours in this game, I can safely say, this game is really overrated. Nothing you choose or do in the game matters. Murder a bunch of Valentinos? They treat you just the same, and Padre wouldn't even bat an eye. Have 5 star police wanted levels? No problem, enter a save zone, in and out and the all the police simultaneously suffers from collective amnesia. The dialogue choice barely matters either, why give me the choice if it doesn't matter? All you're doing is wasting my time making a choice that does nothing. 

And it's not just the lackluster RPG mechanics. The writing in this game is also aggressively mid. The game want us to treat Jackie like an old friend, and want us to feel sad when he dies, but barely give us much time to get to know him personally, how am I supposed to feel for a character that I barely know? Your character V also doesn't have much agencies within the narrative, and by extension a character arc. Not even 1 hour in Johnny immediately hijacks the story and the rest of the story is basically V being taken along for the ride in Johnny's story, hell one of the endings are literally just johnny taking over at the end and V not even being aware of what's going on. V themself also is a very selfish and shallow character, what else does V wanted out of their life other than becoming a legend, get rich, or survive; I really can't find anything else that V values even towards the end. The game does not give me a reason to root for V, and there is also no sense of urgency to V's condition beyond the cutscenes, I just doesn't care about V at all as a character, let alone engage with their story. 

The world building is also extremely generic. Hell it's name literally is just it's genre + 2077, you could not find a game that is more of a parody of cyberpunk than this game. "Oh no! AI will take over!" Yeah like I haven't seen this story already in Terminator, 2001 a Space Odyssey, The Matrix, I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream, Dune, exc... all of them have a deeper exploration into the topic than this game does. And the concept of Rogue AI is also so dumb, like the writer don't understand how technology works, they think AI programs can just "exist" in the magical realm that is the net, without requiring a hardware to run on, like human's can't just locate the server that contains the rogue AI and cut it's power source. And don't even get me started on "Capitalism Bad" and how even more generic and milked to death that topic is. Night City also don't give my any desire to explore it, when basically 95% of the building is just a shell with no interiors, filled with pedestrians that are dumber than a squirrel. Fallout 4 gives me better motivation to explore it's world than this game, and it's literally just a wasteland. There just isn't anything interesting in night city to explore and discover, most of the lore are basically shards with text messages for me to read telling the same generic miserable story about, you guess it, "Capitalism Bad". There is also very little philosophical exploration on the nature of identity, in a game where the story is literally about one person's identity overriding the other, which is just another massive waste of potential in a mountain of wasted potential that is this game. Like imagine V contemplating what it means to be yourself, and questioning rather or not merging with another person's identity is really that bad, like what if instead of Johnny taking over, their identity merges and becomes a whole new person that is neither Johnny or V, imagine the potential of the premise of transferable consciousness and identity, but NO, this game doesn't explore ANY of those possibilities! Ghost in the Shell explore a lot of these topics, so I don't know why they didn't even study one of the most popular cyberpunk franchise out there and learn from it, like I'm not even asking you to have original ideas, at least match the depth of other stories in the same genre! 

I can use two words to summarize this game: Wasted Potential. Choices don't matter, characters don't develop, generic world building, shallow narrative, and I haven't even mention all the unfulfilled promises that they still haven't remotely fulfilled. This game is just too overrated for me to recommend it.

What a ride. The worldbuilding in Cyberpunk is great—it immediately sets the tone for the world you will soon be let loose in, showing the rawness and dystopian nature of Night City. The game covers a lot of subjects, such as politics, the economy, corporations, history, the loss of a loved one, depression, PTSD, and more.

I initially dropped this game somewhere around the end of Act I and returned months later. I decided to start a completely fresh playthrough since I had forgotten a lot of the story. It wasn't until this playthrough that I got the opportunity to appreciate how dynamic the gameplay can be. The Skill Tree allows for a plethora of choices on how YOU want to play Cyberpunk 2077. Want to be a Cyberpsycho with a katana and a Sandy (Sandevistan) to slow down time? Sure. Prefer to be a brute with Gorilla Arms and land explosive punches? Go ahead. Want to be a Skyrim-like stealth archer, but with a silenced pistol? It's here. The gameplay really is GREAT!

I wasn't here when the game was the infamous dumpster fire we all know. But I can testify the game is great now and runs smoothly, especially on a mid-tier setup like mine (specs attached). Easily getting 130-160 FPS.

However, there's something that bugs me, and it's the story pacing. Act I is phenomenal. It introduces the main character, their backstory of your choice, the heist, and [spoiler] Johnny Silverhand—showing the consequences of raw ambition for fame, glory, and riches. [/spoiler]

Personally, the game carries the story well... until the end of Act II. Suddenly, everything just feels very rushed and lackluster once you reach the Point of No Return. I also found, disappointingly, Act III to be extremely short in comparison to the others. I played multiple endings and found most of them just... meh? Like, c'mon. The game kicks off with a bang... literally. But towards the end, it feels like a slow-burning candle with an almost exhausted wick.

Aside from that, I really have nothing negative to say about Cyberpunk 2077. The creativity that went into this is WILD. Props to CD Projekt Red for not doing an Anthem and instead standing behind this project.

I think it's both easy and difficult to describe just how good of a game Cyberpunk 2077 turned out to be from the way I experienced it. In one sentence, Cyberpunk 2077 is probably one of the most well-made, wholeheartedly complete games that exists out there. The entire world of Cyberpunk basically lived by its code of making a name for yourself that it itself spawned a majorly successful anime, collaborations, comics and books, a whole new fandom out of it. Just the CD Projekt effect maybe. 

Else, Cyberpunk 2077 certainly has some flaws that to others may have been the arrow to the knee for them, but I'm going to be describing how I felt. And in spite of the minor flaws it had, as a whole, I felt very, VERY content with it all. 

I spent the past year and a bit playing this game, on and off, taking breaks that were months long before picking it up again, and every time I did, I got right back into the groove of completely absorbing myself into the world of Night City like I never left. Some games when I've played after a certain time away from it, I end up struggling to reconnect. But with Cyberpunk, it never felt like that at all. 

Every character actually had depth. I sympathised with more than one character and wanted to learn of their back stories more than ever. Learning characters back stories? Who would've thought. The side gigs - sure, some of them got repetitive - but they at least were different in that each gig occasionally had motives. They had clues, evidence of something else going on, and at some point Cyberpunk 2077 the action RPG turned into a mystery thriller game. The combat is extremely versatile. I mostly played a Netrunner build for my V with quickhacks and non-confrontational attacks, but when I restarted and decided to go for a mostly Mercenary frontal assault V, it was just as smooth of a transition to be a ruthless killer slicing enemies with katanas and shooting everybody down with the spray of your machine gun. 

I finished the whole game, completed all gigs, got all tarots, played the DLC with all endings through and through, and I can say without a doubt that I'll be remembering Cyberpunk 2077 for a long time. In fact, I know that once I finish this review to go to uninstall this game, I'm actually going to miss it. I intend to keep it as one of my most favourite games of all time for the kind of impact it has on my experience as a gamer towards video games, and if anything, I hope that when people pick this game up or wonder if this game was the right choice to start playing, they haven't seen anything yet.

This game is one of the most fun games I ever played. First person shooters can be pretty hit or miss for me, but this game starts off incredibly fun and it only gets better as you level up. There are a LOT of ways to customize your character, from weapons, to skills, to clothes, and to cyberware, and you can really create some interesting combinations. Plus, there is so much leveling! Normal leveling, plus skill progression, plus street cred! By the end of the game, I'm a powerhouse with armor, health, weapon damage, and resistances, mowing my way through whatever crosses my path.

The main issue is the story SUCKSSSSSSSS. There are fun and interesting parts of the story, but a lot of it is slow and unskippable. I've done the main story all the way through twice, and there are so many dead moments. There is also a lot of slow walking behind someone, sometimes while they explain something you can't skip. There are a lot of times where you have to [spoiler]fight as Johnny, removing any and all upgrades/cyberware/weapons you've gotten but keeping the level difficulty. You get thrown into a completely new playstyle at a high level with no way to manual save! It's the only part of the game I really die in.[/spoiler]

Plus, [spoiler]I love Keanu Reeves, but Johnny is ANNOYING. I liked him the first playthrough, but he actually lies to you/misleads you/misrepresents things a LOT and he shames you for things you have no control over. Plus he bothers you all the time. And your relationship is applied inconsistently. Why am I being forced to say I hate him when I spent the entire game building rapport? Why am I forced to say I like him around when we have no relationship to speak of? There are times where he tells you to do something, and if you don't do it, you're treated like an idiot by the game, and there are times where you are treated like an idiot if you DO listen to him. It's all very confusing and jarring. [/spoiler]

Speaking of characters, Judy and Panam are fine, but the male romance options are TERRIBLE. You have a [spoiler]corrupt cop who tries to play puppy after dragging you through corrupt cop ♥♥♥♥[/spoiler] and then you have [spoiler]the 80 year old rockstar who is still in love with the man in your head who tries to destroy three girls careers because he's a bitter washed up ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.[/spoiler] Plus, both male romance options are side quest locked, so completely missable, while Judy and Panam are met through the main plot.

Heck, even Judy has her problems. Judy [spoiler]is left sad in all endings except one that has nothing to do with her. Why am I becoming distant and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ to her in the mansion ending? My V wouldn't do that?[/spoiler] I haven't finished the Panam romance yet, but it's... weird so far too.

Also, the gigs. There are so many gigs with secret requirements that aren't communicated in anyway. Sometimes it will say "Don't be seen (optional)" but a LOT of times, the game expects you to be stealthy or not kill people or whatever and you only find out at the end of the mission when the fixer is disappointed in you. It happened with EVERY fixer, to the point that I dropped a save before EVERY gig so I could go back and do it again in case of secret expectations.

The biggest sin of the story has got to be the extreme cynicism. By the time I was getting to the end of the game, I knew that if I was going out of my way to save someone, there was a pretty high chance they would [spoiler]kill themselves.[/spoiler] It literally just kept happening. There are so many times where you try so hard to do good things, and it almost feels like the game is laughing at you for trying. I actually really like grimdark, gritty, and cynical media, but this was almost unpalatable in some cases because instead of "everything is literally as bad as possible, but you can do something" it very much has the feeling of "everything is bad and you're stupid for thinking you could make ANYTHING better." There are a couple places where you can do something, but it's mostly punished in my experience.

All this to say, the story is frustrating and mean and painful. There isn't a single ending [spoiler]where you don't die,[/spoiler] which has some foreshadowing, but it really feels like the last f u to [spoiler]give you hope and then show you that it's hopeless.[/spoiler]

The reason I have 184 hours (and why I will almost certainly have more) is that the gameplay is genuinely so fun. I feel like I can recommend this game, despite all the huge issues, because you can literally just not play the story. I have a character right now that I started with phantom liberty, but instead of doing the DLC, I just ran around and did all the NCPD side quests and killed enemies wherever they showed up. That it the real fun of the game. Running around the map with your cool abilities and awesome guns and mindlessly killing stuff to level up. I could, and have, done it for hours, and it's something I've even used to relax.

I would say get this game on sale and be prepared for the slog to get to the good stuff, if you are willing. If you aren't willing to wade through everything above for a fun, brainless, in game murder spree, I don't recommend this game.

I bought Cyberpunk because everyone keeps saying how good the game has become, and honestly, I was just bored out of my mind.

The entire gameplay loop feels like:

Dialogue → walk for 30 seconds → dialogue → walk for another 30 seconds → dialogue → shoot some enemies with some of the worst gunplay I've ever experienced → dialogue → walk for 30 seconds → repeat.

It's just so unbelievably boring.

Don't get me wrong, some of the dialogue is actually interesting, and I can see the appeal of certain story moments. But especially during gameplay missions, the conversations feel incredibly shallow. Characters keep talking at you while you're walking from one objective to another, but most of it feels like filler rather than anything genuinely interesting.

And then there's the dialogue system. You get multiple dialogue options, but most of them feel completely pointless. If you don't pick the obvious main story option, you don't discover anything interesting, unlock a side quest, or get any meaningful alternative outcome. You just get a few extra lines of dialogue before the game forces you back onto the one option that actually progresses the story.

Why even give me the illusion of choice if nothing meaningful comes out of it?

I genuinely don't understand why people enjoy this game so much. Maybe the story gets better later on, but if the gameplay is this tedious, the gunplay feels this bad, and so many dialogue choices feel superficial, I really don't see the appeal.

In terms of worldbuilding and atmosphere, Cyberpunk 2077 might be one of the best games ever. If you're looking for a very story rich game or like Keanu Reeves this is a must play. But the endless dialogue scenes and especially the braindance missions really interrupt the action. Gameplay itself is cool and allows for a lot of customisability, but even on 'very hard' I find it rather easy to just blast through everything before enemies can touch you. If you upgrade your character a bit along the way, it is very easy to simply ignore mechanics. Boss battles are hit or miss, most are simple bullet sponges with high health pools, but some have cool interactions. Side missions are where it's at, definitely don't skip those for both engaging fights and immersive story.

This game is a work of art. With an immersive world and thrilling story. The base game itself is already amazing and the dlc just adds onto that. It has high replayability and customization so no playthrough is exactly the same as your last unless you intend for it to be.

CD Projekt Red never fails to deliver a masterclass in storytelling, and Cyberpunk 2077 stands as an absolute must-play experience.

From the moment you step into Night City, the game pulls you into a beautifully constructed dystopian world. The overarching narrative unfolds gradually, paired with deep, immersive worldbuilding that makes the city feel alive and keeps you coming back for more. What sets it apart, though, is the emotional connection you form with the characters - every decision and conversation feels heavy, meaningful, and grounded. Throughout the entire gameplay loop, you never feel like you are completing filler content just for the sake of checking off a box; every mission carries real narrative weight.

Then comes Phantom Liberty—the ultimate cherry on top. Easily ranking among the best expansion packs ever created, it kicks off with a bang and maintains non-stop momentum straight through to the end.

Seeing where Cyberpunk 2077 started compared to where it sits today is nothing short of incredible. CDPR delivered a legendary gameplay experience, and getting to step into the shoes of V is an journey no RPG fan should miss
